Max Common Chord 3

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Explore two overlapping circles and try to make the crossbar A–B as long as this construction allows.
How to play: Drag P, Q, A or B with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Choose Adjust circles or Adjust chord, then try Show best chord.
Look for the math

This picture comes from a 1975 olympiad problem. Two circles cross at P and Q; a line through P meets them again at A and B. Which line makes the piece AP × PB the longest? Hubert Shutrick found that a moving point S on one auxiliary circle answers the question all at once.

Turn the product into one distance

Here the circles are called C(E) and C(F), with centres E and F. Draw the circle through A, B and Q: it crosses the line PQ again at R. The chords AB and QR cross at P, so the intersecting chords theorem says

AP × PB = PQ × PR

P and Q are fixed once the two circles are given, so making the product biggest is the same as moving R as far from P as possible.

Why QR is twice QN

Let S be the centre of the circle through A, B and Q. The two points Q and R are both one radius from S, so triangle SQR is isosceles. The foot N of the perpendicular from S to PQ is the middle of its base QR, giving

QR = 2 × QN

The live page hides the correct word inside a little quiz: its source shows the choices “twice, twice, thrice, four times”. The construction and the logic test agree that the answer is twice. The test checks this on thousands of chords, not just one.

Where S must sit

As the chord turns, S travels on the circumcircle C(O) of E, Q and F. Let U be the other point where line PQ meets C(O), and T the point opposite Q on that circle, so QT is a diameter. The page says the maximum happens when SN is tangent to C(O), which happens when S bisects the arc from T to U. The applet's own completion test is the same idea in angles: |angle(UQS) − angle(SQT)| < 0.01. The test confirms that at this S the two angles are equal and QN, hence QR and AP × PB, is greatest.

That maximum statement assumes the diagram's order: P lies between Q and U. If you swap the names of P and Q, U moves to the other side and the arc midpoint can give the smallest product instead — the core keeps the applet's arithmetic either way.

What the buttons do

With Adjust chord selected, A and B are kept on the two circles and the other end is pulled back onto its circle so the chord still passes through P. With Adjust circles, dragging A or B redraws that circle instead. Show best chord is a modern shortcut: the original applet had only the two radio buttons and the names checkbox, and you had to find S by dragging.

Try dragging Q until P sits between Q and U, then press Show best chord and compare the two equal arcs at Q.
